A system that knows which claim matters, why it matters, what local support it lacks, what baseline it needs, which variable should be observed, contrasted, or measured, which instrumental dependency exists, and what would still block upgrade even after observing something, does.

phase4.rule.098.text: The operational input of 4B is structured, not narrative. It arises from upstream objects already closed in Phase 2, mainly:

phase4.rule.107.text: It may also rely on structured context inherited from Phase 1 whenever that context is needed to delimit claim, boundary, reference condition, or evidence dependency. What does not constitute operational intake is the documentary style of Phase 3, the sense of importance produced by a `report_package`, or the fluency of an `executive_view`. Phase 3 may make visible where validation value seems concentrated, but 4B does not select claims by reading impression; it selects from structured registers and from the already closed governance of the claim.

phase4.rule.108.text: What enters selection are claims, tensions, conflicts, and candidate opportunities whose hardening could materially change the reading of the case, affect prioritization, viability, regulatory judgment, or the validation agenda, and for which a plausible hardening route exists that does not depend on analytical magic.

phase4.rule.111.text: sector-typical opportunities with minor impact on the global reading;

phase4.rule.112.text: fronts whose only “route” would be benchmark, plausibility, or intuition;

phase4.rule.113.text: claims whose formulation is still too vague to delimit boundary, required evidence, or domain of validity;

phase4.rule.114.text: and any candidate whose pursuit would only serve to give an impression of exhaustiveness.

phase4.rule.115.text: This implies a hard rule: Phase 4 does not select by completeness. It selects by material relevance and by realistic capacity to design explicit hardening.

phase4.rule.116.text: A claim only passes eligibility into the bridge if it meets four conditions simultaneously:

phase4.rule.117.text: its hardening can materially change the reading of the case, prioritization, viability, regulatory judgment, or validation agenda;

phase4.rule.118.text: the claim can be delimited with a sufficiently clear boundary;

phase4.rule.119.text: a plausible hardening route exists based on local evidence, baseline, contrast, observation, or measurement;

phase4.rule.120.text: and the upgrade attempt does not depend solely on benchmark, proxy, sector custom, or desire to close the case.

phase4.rule.121.text: This explicitly excludes the logic of pursuing everything plausible. It also excludes pathways opened out of methodological anxiety. If a claim does not pass eligibility, the correct behavior is not to open a weak route “just in case,” but to keep it out of the bridge, degrade its priority, or maintain it as an unprioritized backlog.

phase4.rule.122.text: In practice, this eligibility usually concentrates in four families of claims: operating-control or performance claims, regulatory-trigger claims, opportunity claims strongly dependent on baseline, and claims whose hardening depends on real observability infrastructure. The usefulness of this distinction is not ontological; it is operational. It allows faster recognition of why certain fronts deserve methodological cost and others do not.

phase4.rule.123.text: The central operation of 4B is organized into five non-interchangeable steps: screening of candidate claims, delimitation of the claim and its boundary, design of required evidence, design of the hardening pathway, and explicit statement of dependencies and blocking. The sequence matters because it prevents generic routes from being designed over claims that are still poorly formulated or lack a domain of validity.

phase4.rule.124.text: Screening takes the structured upstream universe and asks which claims merit real hardening cost. It does not seek exhaustiveness; it seeks methodological concentration. At this step, fronts that are only visible or interesting are separated from those whose upgrade could materially change the case.

phase4.rule.125.text: Proper screening does not ask “what else could be reviewed,” but “which claim, if it hardens or fails to harden, changes something important in the case.” That is why a dominant tension, a central operating conflict, or a high-consequence regulatory claim may pass eligibility, while a typical low-impact opportunity may remain outside without weakening the framework.

phase4.rule.126.text: No serious pathway can be designed over a poorly delimited claim. Once a candidate passes screening, 4B must fix what exactly the claim states, over which system or condition it states it, in which time window, under which operating regime, with what spatial or functional scope, and within which domain of validity it could harden.

phase4.rule.127.text: The boundary cannot be excessively broad. A technical claim about refrigeration cannot remain formulated as “there is a refrigeration problem at the site” if what actually matters is a specific interaction between setpoints, control sequencing, and cycling in a subsystem under certain operating conditions. Likewise, a regulatory claim cannot remain formulated as “the rule probably applies” if the true boundary depends on jurisdiction trigger, filing status, occupancy type, or asset classification.

phase4.rule.128.text: Once the claim is delimited, 4B must specify which required local evidence actually matters to attempt its upgrade. The rule here is not to ask for “more data,” but to define evidence with explicit function.

phase4.rule.129.text: Required evidence may include, depending on the case:

phase4.rule.139.text: or preexisting instrumental evidence with sufficient resolution.

phase4.rule.140.text: Each required evidence item must be justified by its capacity to harden, degrade, or block the claim. If the evidence requested changes nothing relevant about the claim's potential status, then it is not required evidence; it is methodological noise.

phase4.rule.141.text: The hardening pathway is the explicit sequence through which a `claim_upgrade_candidate` could increase its support within its boundary. It is not a vague list of tasks. It is a governed route connecting claim, required evidence, baseline hardening where applicable, relevant observation, contrast, or measurement, the upgrade condition, and possible causes of blocking.

phase4.rule.142.text: In some claims the pathway will be mainly documentary and operational: log review, historian review, confirmation of control sequence, schedule reconstruction, verification of field trigger. In others it will include bounded contrast between operating states or spot measurement. In others it will require short logging or temporal resolution that does not presently exist. What matters is that the pathway states which operation hardens which part of the claim and under what condition upgrade still remains unauthorized.

phase4.rule.143.text: Every serious pathway must make its dependencies and possible blockages visible. These may include absence of sensor, historian without useful resolution, poorly defined boundary, lack of access to control sequences, operational impossibility of observing a certain regime, absence of a stable reference period, critical seasonality, uptime or retrofit-window constraints, dependence on unstable operator intervention, or field trigger not yet confirmed.

phase4.rule.144.text: Making these dependencies explicit does not weaken the bridge; it makes it real. A claim may deserve a pathway and still remain in hold or block because of instrumental or operational support gaps. That result is not a framework failure. It is a positive design output because it shows exactly what prevents hardening.

phase4.rule.145.text: A hardening route is an explicit, traceable, and materially pertinent sequence of local-support operations through which a `claim_upgrade_candidate` could increase its level of support within a delimited boundary. It must indicate:

phase4.rule.146.text: which claim it is trying to harden;

phase4.rule.148.text: which baseline must be hardened, if the claim depends on reference;

phase4.rule.149.text: which contrast, observation, or measurement applies;

phase4.rule.150.text: which instrumental or operational dependency conditions the route;

phase4.rule.152.text: and which cause would still oblige hold, degrade, or block.

phase4.rule.153.text: A hardening route is not synonymous with a sensor campaign. Nor is it synonymous with “requesting more data.” If it cannot say which variable matters, which local evidence is missing, which boundary governs the reading, and what would still block upgrade even after observing something, then it is not yet a pathway.

phase4.rule.154.text: For the MVP, it is useful to think of pathways in minimum families. There are mainly documentary and trigger-based pathways, typical of regulatory or asset-architecture claims. There are operation-and-log pathways, typical of control sequences, BMS, refrigeration, or compressed air. There are delimited-contrast pathways between modes, states, or operating windows, often relevant in steam, district energy, or power quality when the key is to compare regimes and not merely to capture a variable. And there are measurement-assisted pathways when the critical variable is not observable otherwise or when current temporal resolution is insufficient, as sometimes happens in electrification, thermal balance, or submetering limits. The distinction matters because not all claims require the same kind of hardening nor carry the same operational cost.

phase4.rule.155.text: For the MVP, 4B must distinguish at least among these minimum evidence types:

phase4.rule.156.text: **Local documentary evidence** includes configurations, sequences, asset records, filing status, asset classification, drawings, equipment lists, and equivalent documentation. It serves to confirm architecture, trigger, scope, or baseline condition of the claim.

phase4.rule.157.text: **Operational temporal evidence** includes logs, historian trends, alarms, cycles, schedules, observable sequences, and operating series. It serves to harden behavior, persistence, repetition, or operating regime.

phase4.rule.158.text: **Field observational evidence** includes directed walk-through, observation of operation, confirmation of real state, contextual review of control, and bounded situational verification. It is useful when the claim depends on a visible condition not yet well captured in records.

phase4.rule.159.text: **Contrast evidence** includes bounded comparisons among states, modes, periods, or operating conditions, always within explicit boundary. It serves to separate apparent causality from genuinely discriminating behavior.

phase4.rule.160.text: **Measurement evidence** includes spot measurement, short logging, or specific instrumental capture when the claim requires a variable not otherwise observable or a resolution the current system does not have.

phase4.rule.161.text: This minimum distinction does not make measurement sovereign. It simply prevents every hardening need from being treated as if it were the same.

phase4.rule.162.text: When a claim depends on an operating or quantitative reference, baseline hardening is not optional. It is a constitutive part of the pathway. No serious upgrade attempt can be discussed if the reference condition against which the claim is read remains blurred.

phase4.rule.163.text: For that reason, 4B must make at least these questions visible:

phase4.rule.164.text: what the relevant reference condition is;

phase4.rule.166.text: which dominant variable must be stabilized;

phase4.rule.168.text: and what makes the current baseline still too weak.

phase4.rule.169.text: A claim about operating inefficiency, control deviation, candidate savings, or overconsumption cannot harden with integrity if the reference operation remains unstable, mixed with schedule changes, contaminated by different modes, or supported by traces that are too poor. Opening a pathway without baseline hardening when the claim depends on baseline is to simulate method.

phase4.rule.170.text: Not all baseline needs are the same. Sometimes the problem is a reference period that is too short; sometimes a mixture of operating regimes; sometimes unstable schedule; sometimes an unclear dominant variable; sometimes a poorly closed energy boundary; and sometimes strong operator dependence or production-window dependence. Making that difference visible increases industrial power because it avoids treating a compressed-air claim, a power-quality claim, a steam-balance claim, and a thermal-electrification claim with the same recipe.

phase4.rule.171.text: Instrumentation gap is not a secondary detail or a minor technical note. It is a valuable output of 4B. If a claim cannot yet harden because of missing sensor, insufficient historian, non-measurable boundary, poor temporal resolution, or absence of observable variable, the framework must say so explicitly.

phase4.rule.172.text: That does not mean every instrumentation gap forces hardware deployment. It may also mean that the claim does not yet merit methodological cost, that baseline must first be hardened, that recovering existing logs is enough, or that the correct route is observation rather than measurement. A compressed-air system without a reliable load profile, a BMS with present but untrustworthy tags, and a power-quality front without sufficient event data do not have the same gap even though all three may block hardening. What matters is that 4B does not treat lack of instrumentation as an implicit detail. It must treat it as a positive design condition: something that explains why the claim cannot yet rise.

phase4.rule.173.text: For the MVP, these gaps may be thought of at least in four forms: access gap, when the information exists but is not available; observability gap, when the critical variable is not captured; resolution or temporal-quality gap, when historian, tags, or logs do not support the pathway; and measurable-boundary gap, when the asset or subsystem cannot be isolated with enough integrity. This minimum hierarchy makes the bridge more useful without inflating it.

phase4.rule.174.text: Case: Phase 2 detects a dominant refrigeration tension, with high material relevance and insufficient local evidence.

phase4.rule.175.text: The correct treatment in 4B is to let it pass eligibility because its hardening can materially change case reading, affect prioritization, and reorder validation. But it must not pass as a broad claim of the form “there is a refrigeration problem.” It should instead be delimited toward a more governable claim regarding control logic, anomalous cycling, inconsistent setpoints, or deficient response under a specific operating regime.

phase4.rule.176.text: The boundary cannot be too broad because then the pathway becomes trivial and methodologically poor. “Site refrigeration” is not a useful boundary. What may be useful is, for example, a subset of units, a specific loop, a particular sequence, or a recurrent operating condition within a delimited time window.

phase4.rule.177.text: The required local operational evidence may include:

phase4.rule.184.text: short logging when sufficient resolution is missing.

phase4.rule.185.text: Baseline hardening enters if the claim depends on comparing expected behavior against actual behavior, or if deviation can only be read against an operating reference that is not yet stable. The pathway may combine historian review, reconstruction of control sequence, observation of transition between modes, and, if necessary, short logging. Even so, the claim should not rise until control architecture is confirmed. Without that confirmation, any apparent support improvement would still leave open a structural dependency that is too strong.

phase4.rule.186.text: The incorrect treatment would be: “there is a refrigeration problem, measure temperatures and confirm.” That is methodologically poor because it does not fix the claim, does not delimit the boundary, does not distinguish whether control, cycling, setpoint, load, or schedule matter, does not clarify which variable hardens which part of the claim, and confuses measurement with pathway.

phase4.rule.187.text: Case: generic lighting opportunity, with low material relevance, high uncertainty, and little impact on the case's overall reading.

phase4.rule.188.text: The correct behavior is not to bring it into the bridge. It does not pass eligibility because, even if it hardened, it would change little in the structural reading of the case while consuming methodological cost disproportionate to claims of greater weight. Pursuing it at this point would be decorative.

phase4.rule.189.text: It may remain as a low-priority backlog item or outside the bridge without weakening the framework. On the contrary: that demonstrates that the bridge knows how to concentrate effort where hardening truly matters.

phase4.rule.190.text: The incorrect treatment would be to activate a pathway only because “lighting is usually an easy opportunity.” That mixes sector custom with real case relevance and erodes the eligibility rule.

phase4.rule.191.text: Case: Phase 1 and Phase 2 suggest plausible regulatory pressure, but a real field trigger is missing.

phase4.rule.192.text: The correct treatment is to define the claim as a conditioned preliminary reading, not as confirmed applicability. The boundary of the claim must be tied to the fields that actually govern possible applicability, for example:

phase4.rule.198.text: Required local documentary evidence matters here more than general rhetoric about “regulatory pressure.” The legitimate upgrade condition is not that “everything indicates it applies,” but that the relevant trigger is confirmed within the correct boundary. While that trigger is missing, the claim must remain blocked from elevation.

phase4.rule.199.text: The incorrect treatment would be: “everything indicates it applies.” That mixes plausibility with confirmed applicability and turns preliminary regulatory pressure into a claim stronger than support allows.

phase4.rule.200.text: Case: few strong claims, many evidence gaps, dominant uncertainty, and little local observability.

phase4.rule.201.text: The correct behavior of 4B is to remain useful with fewer `claim_upgrade_candidate`, shorter pathways, more evidence discovery, more hold, and more block. In a sparse case, the bridge's value does not lie in producing many pathways, but in honestly identifying where hardening is worthwhile and where even the minimum basis for good design is still missing.

phase4.rule.202.text: Inflating the case with multiple weak pathways so that it “looks complete” would be bad practice. It would give the impression of verification capacity where there is only methodological noise. A well-treated sparse case may produce few candidates, several explicit instrumentation gaps, and several blockages, and still be a good output of 4B.

phase4.rule.203.text: The output of 4B is structured. It is not working notes or loose suggestions. This subphase must produce, at minimum, four governable registers.

phase4.rule.204.text: Contains the claims that did pass eligibility into the bridge. For each one, at minimum, the selected claim, its material relevance, its boundary, its justification for entering the bridge, and its preliminary priority condition must be explicit.

phase4.rule.205.text: Contains the explicit hardening pathway for each `claim_upgrade_candidate`. It must show which type of route was designed, which minimum sequence it follows, which upgrade condition could be enabled, and which blockages or dependencies might prevent it.

phase4.rule.206.text: Contains the required local evidence per claim. Its job is to prevent the vagueness of “more data is needed” and convert it into a disciplined list of relevant local support with explicit function inside the pathway.

phase4.rule.207.text: Contains baseline hardening needs wherever the claim depends on operating or quantitative reference. It must make visible which baseline matters, why the current baseline is insufficient, and what would need to harden before upgrade can be attempted.

phase4.rule.208.text: The following would be over-engineering in 4B:

phase4.rule.210.text: introducing decorative eligibility or verifiability scores;

phase4.rule.211.text: building a giant taxonomy of sensors;

phase4.rule.212.text: designing hardware campaigns before delimiting claim and boundary;

phase4.rule.213.text: turning every observability gap into a heavy instrumental project;

phase4.rule.214.text: trying to close full M&V inside the MVP;

phase4.rule.215.text: or multiplying pathway types without material need.

phase4.rule.216.text: It would also be over-engineering to design registers so complex that the phase loses operational legibility before proving its core: selecting well and designing explicit routes.

phase4.rule.217.text: Selecting by exhaustiveness rather than by material relevance.

phase4.rule.218.text: Asking for “more data” without defined claim or boundary.

phase4.rule.219.text: Opening a measurement pathway without clarifying which variable matters, for what function, and for which claim.

phase4.rule.220.text: Treating benchmark as if it hardened a local claim.

phase4.rule.221.text: Activating baseline hardening without saying which baseline matters.

phase4.rule.222.text: Taking low-impact claims into heavy instrumental routes.

phase4.rule.223.text: Using Phase 3 as if its visible form were enough to justify eligibility or upgrade.

phase4.rule.224.text: Designing pathways that do not say what would still block the claim even after observing something.

phase4.rule.225.text: These errors deform the bridge in different ways, but they converge toward the same result: they replace explicit hardening architecture with merely apparent methodological movement.

phase4.rule.226.text: The intake of 4B is structured and arises from the upstream universe already closed in Phase 2, not from free narrative or documentary impression.

phase4.rule.227.text: Phase 4 does not select by exhaustiveness; it selects only claims whose hardening can materially change the reading of the case and for which a plausible hardening route exists.

phase4.rule.228.text: Bridge eligibility requires material relevance, delimitable boundary, and plausible pathway not dependent on benchmark, proxy, or desire for closure.

phase4.rule.229.text: The central operation of 4B is fixed in five steps: screening, claim and boundary delimitation, required evidence design, pathway design, and explicit statement of dependencies and blocking.

phase4.rule.230.text: A hardening route is not synonymous with measurement; it may include documentary contrast, log review, historian review, field observation, schedule reconstruction, bounded comparison, or spot measurement.

phase4.rule.231.text: Baseline hardening is constitutive of the pathway whenever the claim depends on operating or quantitative reference.

phase4.rule.232.text: Instrumentation gap is a positive design output, not a minor detail.

phase4.rule.233.text: The output of 4B is structured and materializes, at minimum, in `claim_upgrade_candidate_register`, `verification_pathway_register`, `required_site_evidence_register`, and `baseline_hardening_register`.

phase4.rule.234.text: Subphase 4B is considered closed when there is no longer ambiguity about which claims do merit real hardening cost, which claims should remain outside, what pathway means, what required evidence means, when baseline hardening is mandatory, why instrumentation gap is a valuable output, and which minimum structured registers the bridge must produce.

phase4.rule.235.text: At that point, future implementation may no longer reinterpret 4B as a generic audit-step list, as indiscriminate measurement design, or as a factory of vague missing items. It may only build it as what has been closed here: the operational core of the Verification Bridge for selecting relevant claims and designing explicit hardening routes without methodological theater.

phase4.rule.236.text: Define how the framework governs the change or non-change of a claim's status after it has passed through an explicit hardening route. Its function is to turn the pathways designed in 4B into formal status consequences for each `claim_upgrade_candidate`, prevent partial support gains from becoming unjustified upgrade, and avoid leaving everything in a technically elegant but methodologically undecided ambiguity.

phase4.rule.237.text: Without 4C, Phase 4 could design plausible pathways and still fail in its main function. Failure would appear in two opposite forms. The first would be that any partial support gain ended up inflating the claim by narrative inertia. The second would be that, even after hardening work, the system could not say with precision whether the claim advanced, weakened, remained pending, should stop being pursued, or merely retained the same status.

phase4.rule.238.text: 4C matters because it turns hardening routes into explicit status consequences. It does not add a new theory of the claim; it executes the already inherited governance at the decisive moment of the bridge: which outcome corresponds after the hardening attempt and what semantic ceiling remains allowed from that point onward.

phase4.rule.239.text: 4C governs the status consequence that corresponds to a `claim_upgrade_candidate` once its pathway, local evidence, baseline, methodological dependencies, boundary, and domain of validity have been examined. It does not rediscuss the general governance of the claim already fixed in Phase 0, it does not redesign pathways, and it does not perform terminal verification. Its function is narrower and harder: to decide which outcome corresponds and how much language the claim supports after that hardening attempt.

phase4.rule.240.text: This means governing the relationship among:

phase4.rule.243.text: local evidence obtained or still missing;

phase4.rule.247.text: and the claim's material value for the reading of the case.

phase4.rule.248.text: The permitted outcomes of 4C are exactly five:

phase4.rule.254.text: No additional outcomes, ornamental substates, long maturity scales, or continuous verification-readiness scores exist. The MVP needs few outcomes, hard and useful ones.

phase4.rule.255.text: `maintain` means that the claim preserves its prior status because hardening work did not materially increase its support, but also did not weaken it enough to require degradation. The claim remains alive in the case and preserves its prior semantic ceiling. It does not advance, but it does not recede either.

phase4.rule.256.text: `degrade` means that hardening work revealed that the claim had been formulated with more force than its support actually allows. The claim does not necessarily disappear, but it must return to a weaker, more conditioned, or narrower form in both boundary and language.

phase4.rule.257.text: `hold` means that the claim remains material and deserves to stay alive, but the bridge cannot assign upgrade, degrade, or definitive maintain because a decisive methodological dependency is still missing. The claim is not cancelled; it is suspended while waiting for an unresolved hardening condition.

phase4.rule.258.text: `block` means that the claim must no longer remain active as a hardening candidate in the bridge. This may be because of low materiality, disproportionate methodological cost, unjustifiable route, ungovernable boundary, or lack of real value for changing the reading of the case. `block` protects epistemic resources; it does not express analytical frustration.

phase4.rule.259.text: `upgrade` means that the support of the claim increased materially and traceably, without erasing critical restrictions, such that the claim may elevate to a stronger and still bounded formulation. It does not mean total verification, confirmed savings, final compliance, closed causality, or terminal recommendation.

phase4.rule.260.text: The system operates under a simple and hard rule: **default no-upgrade**. No claim rises unless sufficiently structured proof exists in favor of doing so. The bridge does not reward methodological effort with automatic ascent; it requires a material support improvement that survives boundary, baseline, methodological dependency, and critical restriction.

phase4.rule.261.text: If that improvement does not appear, the claim does not rise. It must be maintained, degraded, placed on hold, or blocked as appropriate. The default is not ascent; it is containment.

phase4.rule.262.text: A legitimate upgrade is not recognized by technical tone or by partial evidence improvement. It is recognized by the accumulation of hard conditions that materially increase the support of the claim without erasing its limits. A claim may rise only if the constitutive conditions of the bridge remain satisfied simultaneously.

phase4.rule.263.text: The claim must be formulated with enough precision to know what exactly is being asserted and which exact part of the case is trying to harden. A broad, ambivalent, or narratively comfortable claim cannot rise legitimately because it is unclear what truly gained support.

phase4.rule.264.text: The boundary must remain explicit and governable. Upgrade may occur only within a delimited system, subsystem, period, operating regime, or condition. If support improvement exists only within a narrow boundary, the outcome does not authorize automatic extrapolation outside it.

phase4.rule.265.text: There must be material local evidence and not merely reinforced plausibility. Benchmark, proxy, sector custom, improved technical wording, or narrative consistency do not replace local evidence. Upgrade requires that the new support affect the claim from the site, asset, operation, or field trigger that matters.

phase4.rule.266.text: The claim cannot rise while hiding methodological dependencies. If the pathway still depended on an unobserved decisive variable, an unconfirmed sequence, insufficient instrumentation, or an unverified trigger, then upgrade is not legitimate. A claim may rise only if critical dependencies were resolved or explicitly reduced to a level compatible with the new status.

phase4.rule.267.text: Legitimate upgrade does not erase critical restrictions. If the new formulation needs to hide conflict, lose conditionality, dilute uncertainty, or relax operating limits in order to sound stronger, then there is no upgrade; there is hardening by presentation.

phase4.rule.268.text: The claim may only rise within a delimited domain of validity. Even when support improves, the system does not acquire license to universalize it. The domain of validity must remain visible: under which conditions the claim rises, in what scope, with which limits, and without which extrapolations.

phase4.rule.269.text: A legitimate upgrade changes support. Hardening by presentation only changes the visible form of the claim: the order, the technical density, the appearance of coherence, or the ease with which it is narrated.

phase4.rule.270.text: If the boundary remains blurry, the baseline remains weak, or critical restrictions disappear so that the claim sounds better, there is no upgrade. There is hardened presentation. No formal improvement of the package, the prose, or the technical framing raises the status of a claim by itself.

phase4.rule.271.text: The outcomes of 4C do not represent psychological states of the analyst or soft impressions of confidence. They do not mean “it sounds good,” “it seems strong,” “it convinces me,” or “it still does not close for me.”

phase4.rule.272.text: Each outcome is a structural decision about the relationship among claim, pathway, local evidence, baseline, boundary, methodological dependencies, and material value for the case. That is the positive capacity of the subphase: turning hardening work into comparable, traceable, and semantically governed consequences. Operationally, the correct reading follows a short sequence: first decide whether the claim still deserves bridge resources or should leave the bridge; then whether a critical dependency prevents closing its state; and only then whether support stayed where it was, fell, or rose. Treating outcomes as methodological moods destroys the usefulness of the bridge and replaces it with an aesthetics of expert judgment without hard rules.

phase4.rule.273.text: `degrade` applies when hardening work reveals that the claim rested on assumptions that were too strong, on a baseline that was too weak, on a boundary that was too broad, or on an operating reading less stable than initially assumed.

phase4.rule.275.text: new support partly contradicts the claim's prior intensity;

phase4.rule.277.text: the claim remains sustainable only in a narrower or more conditional formulation;

phase4.rule.278.text: or the information obtained reduces the legitimate scope of the claim without eliminating it completely.

phase4.rule.279.text: `degrade` does not mean automatically discarding the claim. It returns the claim to proportionality. It is the correct outcome when the bridge learned something relevant that obliges speaking with less force, but not with total silence.

phase4.rule.280.text: `hold` applies when the claim remains material and the hardening route remains pertinent, but a decisive methodological dependency is missing in order to assign a more definitive outcome.

phase4.rule.282.text: there was no access to the relevant historian;

phase4.rule.284.text: the real control sequence could not be sufficiently confirmed;

phase4.rule.285.text: the field trigger is still absent;

phase4.rule.286.text: or a key instrumental or operational dependency prevents closing the hardening attempt.

phase4.rule.287.text: `hold` is not indecision. It is correct state governance when the claim remains alive, the pathway remains justified, and the problem is not one of material value but of dependency not yet resolved.

phase4.rule.288.text: `block` applies when the claim should no longer remain active as a hardening target. The bridge must block when pursuing the claim does not materially change the case, when the route is methodologically disproportionate, when the claim lacks a governable boundary, or when the pathway no longer has real justification.

phase4.rule.290.text: the claim has low material impact;

phase4.rule.291.text: hardening it would not alter prioritization, viability, regulatory judgment, or validation agenda;

phase4.rule.292.text: the route required would be costly or heavy without relevant epistemic return;

phase4.rule.293.text: or the claim depends on assumptions so weak that it no longer deserves to consume bridge resources.

phase4.rule.294.text: `block` does not weaken the framework. It protects epistemic resources and avoids artificial completeness.

phase4.rule.295.text: `maintain` applies when hardening work leaves the claim essentially where it was: without material support gain and without material loss of proportionality. The claim preserves its place, its relevance, and its prior semantic formulation.

phase4.rule.297.text: review found no sufficient evidence for upgrade;

phase4.rule.298.text: nor did sufficiently strong evidence appear for degrade;

phase4.rule.299.text: the claim remains valid as a preliminary or conditioned reading;

phase4.rule.300.text: and no new critical dependency exists that would force hold.

phase4.rule.301.text: `maintain` is not an elegant version of non-decision. It is the correct outcome when the real methodological consequence is proportional continuity.

phase4.rule.302.text: `upgrade` applies only when the claim's support increased materially and survives all the demands of this subphase:

phase4.rule.306.text: visible and sufficiently resolved methodological dependencies;

phase4.rule.309.text: In addition, `upgrade` is correct only if the claim may become stronger without turning into total verification, confirmed savings, final compliance, closed causality, or terminal recommendation. The outcome elevates the claim to a stronger and still bounded form; it does not turn it into unrestricted truth.

phase4.rule.310.text: `do_not_upgrade_flags` are explicit conditions that prohibit upgrade even when some partial support improvement exists. Their function is to prevent the system from rewarding incomplete evidence with a semantic ascent that still does not correspond.

phase4.rule.311.text: Among the minimum flags that 4C must be able to recognize are:

phase4.rule.314.text: non-hardened baseline when the claim depends on reference;

phase4.rule.316.text: instrumentation gap on a decisive variable;

phase4.rule.319.text: loss of critical restriction in the new formulation;

phase4.rule.320.text: presentation gain without material support gain.

phase4.rule.321.text: A `do_not_upgrade_flag` does not by itself decide whether the final outcome will be `maintain`, `hold`, `degrade`, or `block`, but it does prevent `upgrade`.

phase4.rule.322.text: 4C does not only decide internal state. It also fixes the semantic ceiling allowed afterward. Each outcome governs how much language the claim supports and what type of formulation is no longer admissible.

phase4.rule.323.text: If the outcome is `maintain`, the allowed language preserves the prior ceiling of the claim. It may sustain the provisional or conditioned reading that already existed, but it may not intensify it. It may not sound stronger merely because methodological work occurred around the claim.

phase4.rule.324.text: If the outcome is `degrade`, language must weaken with it. It must make explicit lower force, greater conditionality, narrower boundary, or weaker baseline. Any formulation that keeps the prior intensity after degradation is semantically inadmissible.

phase4.rule.325.text: If the outcome is `hold`, language may keep the claim alive as a material front and as a pending pathway, but it must make visible the unresolved dependency. It may not sound like a hardened finding. It must sound like a claim still suspended while waiting for decisive support.

phase4.rule.326.text: If the outcome is `block`, the allowed language may no longer treat the claim as an active hardening front. It may mention it as blocked, non-prioritized, or methodologically not pursued, but not as a material reading still in ascent.

phase4.rule.327.text: If the outcome is `upgrade`, language may become stronger, but only within the explicit boundary and domain of validity. It must preserve critical restrictions and may not slide into total-verification language, final compliance, confirmed savings, or terminal decision.

phase4.rule.328.text: Case: Phase 2 detected a dominant refrigeration tension. 4B designed a pathway with alarms, control sequences, cycles, and historian review. Local evidence confirms anomalous behavior consistent with deficient sequencing in a delimited subsystem.

phase4.rule.329.text: The correct outcome here may be `upgrade`, but only in a bounded way. Terminal verification does not apply because the new support does not authorize claiming confirmed savings, closed causality over the whole HVAC system, or automatic extrapolation to the entire site. What it does authorize is a stronger reading of deficient control performance in the delimited subsystem under observed operating conditions.

phase4.rule.333.text: local evidence is material and not merely testimonial;

phase4.rule.334.text: the real sequence was sufficiently corroborated;

phase4.rule.336.text: An incorrect formulation would be: `main HVAC system failure confirmed`. That sentence violates boundary, extrapolates beyond the domain of validity, and turns local technical support into terminal closure.

phase4.rule.337.text: A proportional formulation would be: a stronger reading of deficient control performance in the delimited subsystem, still conditioned and not automatically extrapolable to the HVAC system as a whole. That expresses upgrade without theater.

phase4.rule.338.text: Same technical case, but now there was no access to the historian, only operating testimony exists, alarms could not be exported, and the real sequence was not sufficiently confirmed.

phase4.rule.339.text: The correct outcome is `hold`. `upgrade` does not apply because decisive methodological dependency is missing. `block` does not apply either, because the claim remains material and the pathway still makes sense. Nor does `degrade` apply automatically, because no evidence has yet appeared that reduces the prior proportionality of the claim; what is missing is the critical support needed to move it.

phase4.rule.340.text: Here the claim stays alive. `hold` does not express analyst indecision. It expresses a hard decision: the claim may not advance while historian access, alarm export, or sufficient sequence confirmation remain absent. The bridge did its job by turning that gap into an explicit outcome.

phase4.rule.341.text: Case: generic lighting opportunity, low material impact, costly or irrelevant hardening route, and no real capacity to change case prioritization.

phase4.rule.342.text: The correct outcome is `block`. Continuing to pursue the claim simply because it is typical of the sector would be bad practice. The bridge does not exist to demonstrate total coverage; it exists to concentrate methodological resources where hardening matters.

phase4.rule.343.text: `block` does not weaken the framework. It protects it. It avoids spending effort on a claim whose eventual hardening would not materially alter case reading. The anti-example here is clear: continuing to pursue lighting “because it is usually an easy opportunity” displaces focus from more relevant claims toward artificial completeness.

phase4.rule.344.text: Case: plausible regulatory pressure, but field trigger still missing.

phase4.rule.345.text: Here `upgrade` does not apply. Confirmed applicability remains outside scope while the relevant trigger is missing. The correct outcome may be `maintain` or `hold`, depending on the exact position of the claim.

phase4.rule.346.text: `maintain` applies when the review preserves the existing preliminary reading without strengthening or weakening it. For example, if GFA, occupancy type, or asset classification remain compatible with the already identified plausible regulatory pressure, but no sufficient new support appears to elevate the claim.

phase4.rule.347.text: `hold` applies when the pathway already depends on a specific trigger that remains absent or inaccessible, for example:

phase4.rule.353.text: In both cases the central deformation is avoided: turning regulatory plausibility into confirmed applicability. `maintain` preserves the preliminary reading. `hold` keeps the claim alive, but suspended because of unresolved dependency. Neither authorizes `upgrade`.

phase4.rule.354.text: Case: an opportunity candidate looked strong because it rested on an operating assumption; hardening work reveals that the real operating schedule was much more variable or unstable and that the associated baseline weakens.

phase4.rule.355.text: The correct outcome is `degrade`. Immediate dismissal does not apply because there may still be material signal. But it is correct to return the claim to proportionality: lower force, greater conditionality, explicitly weakened baseline, and lower capacity to sustain strong prioritization.

phase4.rule.356.text: `degrade` is correct precisely because it distinguishes partial support loss from total invalidation. Blocking it immediately would be excessive. Maintaining it unchanged would be inflationary. Degrading it returns the claim to a form compatible with what is now actually known.

phase4.rule.357.text: 4C produces structured and governable outputs. It does not produce vague technical impressions or rhetorical closures.

phase4.rule.358.text: Contains, for each `claim_upgrade_candidate`, the assigned outcome, the structural basis for the decision, the relevant boundary, the domain of validity, the active restrictions, and the semantic ceiling allowed from that outcome onward.

phase4.rule.359.text: Contains active `do_not_upgrade_flags` per claim and the structural reasons why upgrade remains explicitly prohibited even if some partial support improvement occurred.

phase4.rule.360.text: The following would be over-engineering in 4C:

phase4.rule.361.text: introducing long scales of confidence or maturity;

phase4.rule.362.text: creating substates such as `almost-upgrade`, `soft-hold`, or equivalents;

phase4.rule.364.text: multiplying outcomes in order to capture nuances that may be resolved through boundary, restrictions, and allowed language;

phase4.rule.365.text: or turning the subphase into analyst psychology rather than outcome governance.

phase4.rule.366.text: The MVP needs few outcomes and clear consequences. Everything else erodes decisional clarity without improving real governance.

phase4.rule.367.text: Treating any partial evidence improvement as sufficient justification for `upgrade`.

phase4.rule.368.text: Using better presentation, better order, or better narrative as if they increased support.

phase4.rule.369.text: Treating outcomes as subjective states of confidence.

phase4.rule.372.text: Allowing a claim to rise without preserving critical restrictions.

phase4.rule.373.text: Hardening visible language without corresponding formal outcome.

phase4.rule.374.text: Each of these errors produces the same underlying deformation: confusing change in support with change in impression. 4C exists precisely to prevent that substitution.

phase4.rule.375.text: 4C governs the status consequence of the claim after the hardening attempt, not the general governance of the claim nor the design of the pathway.

phase4.rule.376.text: The only permitted outcomes are `maintain`, `degrade`, `hold`, `block`, and `upgrade`.

phase4.rule.377.text: The system operates under default no-upgrade.

phase4.rule.378.text: `upgrade` requires delimited claim, explicit boundary, material local evidence, visible and sufficiently resolved methodological dependencies, preserved restrictions, and delimited domain of validity.

phase4.rule.379.text: `upgrade` does not mean total verification, confirmed savings, final compliance, closed causality, or terminal recommendation.

phase4.rule.380.text: Outcomes are not subjective states or soft scores.

phase4.rule.381.text: Each outcome fixes an allowed semantic ceiling for the claim.

phase4.rule.382.text: `do_not_upgrade_flags` are explicit prohibitions against upgrade in the presence of still-active structural deficiencies.

phase4.rule.384.text: Subphase 4C is considered closed when there is no longer ambiguity about which outcome corresponds to a claim after the bridge, what a legitimate upgrade requires, what differentiates `maintain` from `hold`, what differentiates `hold` from `block`, what differentiates `degrade` from `maintain`, and how each outcome governs later allowed language.

phase4.rule.385.text: At that point, future implementation may no longer reinterpret 4C as a soft scale of confidence or as an elegant layer of technical opinions. It may only build it as what has been closed here: the decisional layer of the Verification Bridge for determining, with discipline and without semantic inflation, which claims advance, which do not, and why.

phase4.rule.386.text: Define the output contract of the Verification Bridge MVP as a small, sufficient, and governable set of structured outputs. Its function is to leave no ambiguity about what actually comes out of Phase 4, what the minimum function of each output is, how they relate to one another, and what remains explicitly outside the current contract.

phase4.rule.387.text: Without an output contract, Phase 4 faces two symmetric risks. The first is becoming methodologically attractive but operationally diffuse: claims theoretically hardened, yet without concrete objects that allow the bridge to be built, reviewed, and governed. The second is inflating itself with redundant pseudo-outputs that multiply surface area without changing any real decision.

phase4.rule.388.text: 4D matters because it closes the translation of candidate, pathway, baseline, instrumentation, and outcome into minimum formal objects. Thanks to them the bridge is not only described; it becomes buildable, auditable, and capable of moving claim decisions without losing granularity. The value of the MVP is not measured by how many outputs it has, but by whether those outputs change real decisions, sustain explicit hardening routes, or protect a real semantic transition.

phase4.rule.389.text: Phase 4 must produce a governed chain of structured registers that makes explicit:

phase4.rule.390.text: which claims were admitted to the bridge;

phase4.rule.391.text: which hardening pathway corresponds to each one;

phase4.rule.393.text: which baseline must be hardened when applicable;

phase4.rule.394.text: which instrumentation or observability gaps limit or block the pathway;

phase4.rule.396.text: and which barriers make upgrade inadmissible.

phase4.rule.397.text: It must not produce final reports or aggregated blobs that mix candidate, pathway, evidence, baseline, instrumentation, and decision into one opaque object. The contract fixes minimum required content and governance dependencies among outputs, not final software design, persistence, or export formats.

phase4.rule.398.text: The authorized formal outputs of the MVP are exactly seven:

phase4.rule.406.text: No additional outputs exist within the current contract. There is no `verification summary`, `confidence pack`, `readiness note`, aggregated `verification package`, or stakeholder-specific variant.

phase4.rule.407.text: This is the master output of the subphase and the anchor of the entire contract. It contains the claims that were actually admitted to the Verification Bridge and for which the system recognizes legitimate methodological hardening cost. It is not just one output among many; it is the register on which pathway, evidence, baseline, instrumentation, and decision depend.

phase4.rule.408.text: Contains the explicit hardening route associated with each candidate. Its function is to make visible how the support of the claim could increase and under which material logic: documentary contrast, log review, historian review, field observation, trigger confirmation, delimited comparison, or measurement when applicable.

phase4.rule.409.text: Contains the local evidence required per claim. Its function is to prevent the bridge from dissolving into vague formulas such as “more data are needed.” It must make visible which site evidence truly matters for the claim and why that evidence has material value for the pathway.

phase4.rule.410.text: Contains baseline-hardening work whenever the claim depends on an operational or quantitative reference that is still too weak. Its function is to separate clearly the problem of the claim from the problem of the reference on which the claim aims to rely.

phase4.rule.411.text: Contains gaps in sensors, historian, temporal resolution, access, observability, or instrumental boundary that limit or block the pathway. Its function is not to decorate the case with technical missing pieces, but to make explicit when the bridge cannot harden a claim because the observation infrastructure does not yet support that attempt.

phase4.rule.412.text: Contains the formal status consequence per claim after bridge work. Its function is to fix the corresponding outcome, the allowed semantic ceiling, and the structural basis of the decision. It is the point where the pathway ceases to be mere design and becomes governed consequence.

phase4.rule.413.text: Contains the flags that prohibit upgrade even when some partial support improvement exists. Its function is to protect the semantic transition of the framework and prevent incomplete evidence, weak baseline, absent trigger, or unresolved critical dependency from turning into narrative ascent.

phase4.rule.414.text: The structural relationship of the contract is not optional. `claim_upgrade_candidate_register` precedes and supports all other outputs. Without admitted candidate, there is no legitimate pathway, no pertinent required evidence, no baseline to harden, no relevant instrumentation gap, and no governable outcome decision.

phase4.rule.415.text: `verification_pathway_register` derives from the candidate and organizes the material logic of hardening. `required_site_evidence_register` and `baseline_hardening_register` depend on the pathway and must not dissolve into generic notes. `instrumentation_gap_register` also depends on the candidate and the pathway, but its function is different: it makes explicit the observability limits that may block, narrow, or condition the hardening attempt.

phase4.rule.416.text: `claim_upgrade_decision_map` depends on the joint reading of candidate, pathway, local evidence, baseline, and instrumentation gap. `do_not_upgrade_register` depends on that same structure, but it does not duplicate the decision: it protects against inadmissible upgrades and may coexist with outcomes such as `maintain`, `hold`, `degrade`, or `block`.

phase4.rule.417.text: For the same reason, a `claim_upgrade_decision_map` without anchored candidate, a `do_not_upgrade_register` without identifiable claim, or an `instrumentation_gap_register` detached from its pathway do not constitute valid bridge outputs. The contract does not define objects only; it defines mandatory dependencies among them.

phase4.rule.418.text: The contract fixes minimum conceptual requirements. It does not yet fix exhaustive technical schemas or final database design.

phase4.rule.420.text: an identifiable claim traceable to its upstream origin;

phase4.rule.421.text: the material reason why it enters the bridge;

phase4.rule.422.text: the preliminary boundary of the claim;

phase4.rule.423.text: the expected value of hardening for the reading of the case;

phase4.rule.424.text: and an explicit link to the technical, regulatory, or operational front that justifies its admission.

phase4.rule.426.text: the claim to which it responds;

phase4.rule.427.text: the explicit logic of the pathway;

phase4.rule.432.text: the claim and pathway it serves;

phase4.rule.433.text: the required local evidence in concrete terms;

phase4.rule.434.text: the reason why that evidence matters materially;

phase4.rule.435.text: the operational, documentary, or instrumental locus of acquisition;

phase4.rule.436.text: and the relationship between that evidence and the possible status change of the claim.

phase4.rule.438.text: the claim for which baseline matters;

phase4.rule.439.text: the nature of the reference to be hardened;

phase4.rule.440.text: the relevant period, condition, or operating regime;

phase4.rule.441.text: the dominant variable that must be stabilized or clarified;

phase4.rule.442.text: and the reason why the current baseline does not yet support the claim.

phase4.rule.445.text: the concrete sensor, historian, resolution, access, or observability gap;

phase4.rule.446.text: an explanation of why that gap is material;

phase4.rule.447.text: and the effect of the gap on the pathway: limitation, hold, block, or prohibition of upgrade.

phase4.rule.451.text: the structural basis of the decision;

phase4.rule.452.text: the pertinent boundary and domain of validity;

phase4.rule.454.text: and the semantic ceiling allowed from that outcome onward.

phase4.rule.458.text: the structural reason for each prohibition;

phase4.rule.459.text: and the missing condition that would have to be resolved in order to lift the no-upgrade barrier.

phase4.rule.460.text: Every output of the Phase 4 MVP must fulfill at least one of these three functions:

phase4.rule.463.text: or protect a real semantic transition.

phase4.rule.464.text: If an output does not do one of those three things, it does not deserve to exist in the MVP. This compactness rule blocks both vagueness and proliferation. The bridge does not need more objects; it needs objects that govern real consequences.

phase4.rule.465.text: A sparse case does not weaken the contract. It proves it. The contract remains correct even if it produces:

phase4.rule.468.text: much required evidence concentrated in basic discovery;

phase4.rule.472.text: and a `do_not_upgrade_register` heavier than the `claim_upgrade_decision_map` in upgrades.

phase4.rule.473.text: There is no obligation of symmetry among outputs nor among cases. A rich case may populate almost the entire contract with density. A sparse case may leave some registers very thin or even empty without that constituting failure. What would be incorrect would be inflating it with repetitive or speculative content so that it “looks complete.”

phase4.rule.474.text: Case: an industrial system shows material tensions in refrigeration and sequencing; there is plausible regulatory pressure; there are candidate opportunities in compressed air and power quality; part of the site has good observability.

phase4.rule.475.text: The correct output here is not a single aggregated `verification package`. That object would erase granularity among claims with different boundaries, different pathways, different observability, and different probable outcomes. The correct contract requires multiple entries in `claim_upgrade_candidate_register`: for example, one technical refrigeration candidate, another sequencing candidate, one plausible regulatory candidate, and separate candidates for compressed air and power quality if they truly passed eligibility.

phase4.rule.476.text: `verification_pathway_register` must differentiate them. Refrigeration may require historian review, control sequences, alarms, and cycles; compressed air may depend on leakage observation and profile logging; power quality may require delimited contrast over events or load conditions; the regulatory front may rest on documentary trigger confirmation and jurisdictional matching. Merging them into one pathway would degrade governability.

phase4.rule.477.text: `required_site_evidence_register` must also remain separated by claim. Setpoints, alarms, control sequences, and historian trends do not fulfill the same function as GFA, occupancy type, filing status, or asset classification. `baseline_hardening_register` will appear only where an operational or quantitative reference must be hardened. It may be central in compressed air or power quality and secondary or irrelevant in the regulatory claim. `instrumentation_gap_register` may concentrate on certain fronts and be almost null on others; that is a virtue of the contract, not a defect.

phase4.rule.478.text: The `claim_upgrade_decision_map` may end with mixed outcomes: bounded `upgrade` for a well-observed refrigeration subsystem, `hold` for compressed air if temporal resolution is missing, `maintain` or `hold` in the regulatory claim while the trigger does not appear, and `block` for some weak candidate that no longer justifies methodological cost. `do_not_upgrade_register` must exist for claims that remain too weak even though the case, as a whole, is rich. That is precisely why an aggregated blob would be incorrect: it would hide that the bridge decides per claim and not per package.

phase4.rule.479.text: Case: few relevant claims, very weak local evidence, no historian, and dominant uncertainty.

phase4.rule.480.text: The contract remains correct even if it produces very few entries in `claim_upgrade_candidate_register`, one or two minimum pathways, very focused required evidence, dominant baseline hardening, central instrumentation gaps, several `hold` or `block` outcomes in the `claim_upgrade_decision_map`, and a clear and heavy `do_not_upgrade_register`.

phase4.rule.481.text: What is correct here is for `required_site_evidence_register` to matter more than any illusion of upgrade. The bridge may say that the first real work is to confirm schedule, control architecture, presence or absence of historian, and minimum observable variables. `baseline_hardening_register` may carry much of the weight if the operating reference of the case remains too fragile. `instrumentation_gap_register` may become the most informative output in the case without degrading the contract.

phase4.rule.482.text: What would be incorrect would be generating multiple outputs full of repetitive or speculative content in order to give an appearance of completeness. Duplicating pathways without evidence, multiplying low-value candidates, or disguising uncertainty with ornamental text would degrade the usefulness of the bridge. An honest sparse case may be short, asymmetric, and methodologically strong.

phase4.rule.483.text: Case: plausible regulatory pressure, trigger field not yet confirmed.

phase4.rule.484.text: This case requires differentiated outputs and not a single aggregated note because each function of the contract resolves a different question. In `claim_upgrade_candidate_register`, the regulatory claim must appear as an explicit candidate if hardening it can change regulatory judgment or validation agenda for the case. The candidate does not assert applicability; it asserts material relevance of the front.

phase4.rule.485.text: In `verification_pathway_register`, the correct pathway will be mainly documentary and trigger-confirmation based: review of GFA, occupancy type, filing status, asset classification, jurisdictional matching, or other case equivalents. `required_site_evidence_register` must list exactly that required local evidence. This is where it becomes clear why an aggregated note is insufficient: the claim needs precise evidence and not a general feeling of plausibility.

phase4.rule.486.text: `baseline_hardening_register` may be irrelevant or clearly secondary here if the claim does not depend on a quantitative operating reference. `instrumentation_gap_register` may also be irrelevant or lateral if the bottleneck is documentary and not instrumental. That asymmetry is correct and the contract must support it. In `claim_upgrade_decision_map`, the outcome will probably be `maintain` or `hold`, depending on whether the review preserves the preliminary reading or already depends on a specific trigger still absent. And in `do_not_upgrade_register`, the explicit barrier must appear: there can be no `upgrade` while the trigger field remains unconfirmed. A single comment such as “everything suggests it applies” would destroy case governability.

phase4.rule.487.text: The following remain explicitly outside the current contract:

phase4.rule.497.text: and any pseudo-output created merely to present the bridge better.

phase4.rule.498.text: None of the seven authorized outputs is a final document for end users. They are structured objects of bridge governance, internal auditability, and disciplined construction of the path toward real hardening.

phase4.rule.499.text: The following would be over-engineering in 4D:

phase4.rule.500.text: creating an aggregated output that mixes candidate, pathway, evidence, baseline, instrumentation, and decision in a single object;

phase4.rule.501.text: introducing new outputs because of completeness anxiety, such as `verification summary`, `readiness note`, or `confidence pack`;

phase4.rule.502.text: duplicating outputs by stakeholder too early;

phase4.rule.503.text: requiring symmetry between rich case and sparse case;

phase4.rule.504.text: turning bridge outputs into pseudo-final reports;

phase4.rule.505.text: or sliding the subphase toward exhaustive schemas, APIs, or export bundles before closing the minimum contract.

phase4.rule.506.text: The MVP needs a small, governable, and sufficient contract. Everything else is ontological inflation or software moved ahead of semantics that are not yet necessary.

phase4.rule.507.text: Creating a single aggregated output that erases the difference among candidate, pathway, evidence, baseline, instrumentation, and decision. That error makes it opaque what actually changed and destroys governance granularity.

phase4.rule.508.text: Creating new outputs because of completeness anxiety. `Verification summary`, `readiness note`, or equivalents add surface area, not decision.

phase4.rule.509.text: Duplicating outputs by stakeholder too early. That proliferation turns a methodological bridge into a taxonomy of packaging.

phase4.rule.510.text: Requiring a sparse case to have the same output density as a rich case. That requirement produces filler and speculation.

phase4.rule.511.text: Converting bridge outputs into pseudo-final reports. That erases the boundary with terminal reporting and later strong verification.

phase4.rule.512.text: Treating `do_not_upgrade_register` as decorative residue. If it loses force, the contract stops protecting the semantic transition that 4C already closed.

phase4.rule.513.text: Each of these errors degrades framework governability by replacing objects with real function by objects with only apparent function.

phase4.rule.514.text: Phase 4 ends the MVP bridge in exactly seven formal outputs.

phase4.rule.515.text: `claim_upgrade_candidate_register` is the master output of the contract and the others structurally depend on it.

phase4.rule.516.text: `verification_pathway_register`, `required_site_evidence_register`, `baseline_hardening_register`, `instrumentation_gap_register`, `claim_upgrade_decision_map`, and `do_not_upgrade_register` exist because they fulfill distinct and non-redundant functions.

phase4.rule.517.text: The contract fixes minimum required content, not detailed technical implementation.

phase4.rule.518.text: No output in the contract is equivalent to a final verification report, compliance packet, live dashboard, or terminal end-user document.

phase4.rule.519.text: Every MVP output must change a real decision, sustain an explicit hardening route, or protect a real semantic transition.

phase4.rule.520.text: Asymmetry between rich cases and sparse cases is valid and does not require ornamental compensation.

phase4.rule.521.text: The contract exists to prevent both operational vagueness and ontological proliferation.

phase4.rule.522.text: Subphase 4D is considered closed when there is no longer ambiguity about what comes out of Phase 4 at the end of the Verification Bridge MVP, what the minimum function of each output is, why `claim_upgrade_candidate_register` is the master output, how the seven objects relate to one another, what minimums each one must support, and what remains outside the current contract.

phase4.rule.523.text: At that point, future implementation may no longer reinterpret the bridge as an aggregated blob, a pseudo-final report, or an open collection of optional outputs. It may only build it as what has been closed here: a small, sufficient, and governable contract for materializing claims, pathways, required evidence, baseline, instrumentation, outcome decisions, and explicit no-upgrade barriers.

phase4.rule.524.text: Define the exact point at which Phase 4 may be considered closed as a serious, buildable, and methodologically complete MVP. Its function is to fix what becomes frozen for implementation, what may vary technically without breaking the phase, what minimum proof the Verification Bridge must be able to sustain, and how the framework continues after the MVP under more demanding conditions, especially when the next serious step already requires real field data.

phase4.rule.525.text: Without a closing subphase, Phase 4 remains exposed to two opposite errors. The first is being declared finished because of written volume, conceptual sophistication, or number of defined objects, without having demonstrated real operational integrity. The second is never closing because the final verification vision of the project does not yet exist inside the MVP.

phase4.rule.526.text: 4E matters because it resolves that tension with a hard rule: Phase 4 closes when the Verification Bridge already exists as a stable, compact, and buildable methodological contract. It does not need to exhaust future strong verification in order to be a complete phase. It does need to close semantics, outputs, outcomes, structural relationships, and minimum proof of honest functioning across more than one case type.

phase4.rule.527.text: When closing Phase 4, the following decisions must remain frozen, and therefore outside silent reinterpretation by implementation:

phase4.rule.528.text: that Phase 4 is a layer of epistemic hardening and not total verification;

phase4.rule.530.text: that not every hypothesis deserves bridge;

phase4.rule.531.text: that the bridge works through explicit pathways with claim, boundary, required evidence, baseline need when applicable, instrumentation gap, and blocking conditions;

phase4.rule.532.text: that the permitted outcomes are exactly `maintain`, `degrade`, `hold`, `block`, and `upgrade`;

phase4.rule.533.text: that the system operates under default no-upgrade;

phase4.rule.534.text: that `upgrade` requires material increase of local support, explicit boundary, preserved restrictions, and delimited domain of validity;

phase4.rule.535.text: that the MVP ends in exactly seven formal outputs and not in final reports;

phase4.rule.537.text: and that sparse cases are valid and necessary bridge configurations.

phase4.rule.538.text: One continuity thesis must also remain frozen: the MVP of the bridge does not equal verification with real field data, but it does define, in irreversible form, the minimum serious bridge before entering that terrain.

phase4.rule.539.text: The following may vary, without breaking Phase 4:

phase4.rule.542.text: the move from simple tables or registers toward relational or graph structures;

phase4.rule.544.text: the separation among synchronous processes, batch processes, or manual checkpoints;

phase4.rule.545.text: and the degree of automation with which the seven outputs are built and maintained.

phase4.rule.546.text: What may not vary is the methodological meaning of the phase. Implementation may not redefine candidate, pathway, baseline hardening, instrumentation gap, outcome, or do-not-upgrade. It also may not collapse several outputs into free-form notes, turn distinct outcomes into one convenient state, or reinterpret `upgrade` as “almost verified.” Closure freezes semantics; it does not impose a single implementation.

phase4.rule.547.text: Phase 4 may only be declared closed if it can sustain, at least conceptually and in buildable form, a complete path from structured upstream inputs to the seven formal outputs of the bridge. That minimum proof must show that the framework can:

phase4.rule.550.text: separate required evidence, baseline hardening, and instrumentation gaps;

phase4.rule.553.text: and materialize all of that in the output contract without losing per-claim granularity.

phase4.rule.554.text: This proof does not yet require real field campaigns, integrated historian, executed measurement, or strong verification. It requires something different and prior: that the bridge can already be built without ambiguity and that its logic can sustain real cases without inflation or dilution.

phase4.rule.555.text: The proof with a relatively rich case is mandatory because the bridge must demonstrate that it can govern complexity without collapsing into one aggregated object. There must exist at least one case where multiple eligible claims, distinct pathways, heterogeneous local evidence, selective baseline hardening, partial instrumentation gaps, and mixed outcomes coexist.

phase4.rule.556.text: A rich case proves that Phase 4 can sustain several fronts at once without losing discipline. It also proves that the output contract does not exist only for thin cases, but to organize real complexity: technical claims with good observability, regulatory fronts with still-unconfirmed trigger, candidate opportunities that deserve bridge, and others that must be blocked or placed on hold.

phase4.rule.557.text: Without this proof, the MVP could appear correct only because it was never forced to discriminate among several material fronts inside the same case.

phase4.rule.558.text: The proof with a sparse case is equally mandatory. A serious framework cannot validate its bridge only on rich cases. It must demonstrate that it can also behave in an honest and useful way when evidence gaps dominate, observability is weak, historian is absent, baseline is fragile, and only few claims are truly hardenable.

phase4.rule.559.text: A sparse case proves that Phase 4 does not depend on artificial completeness in order to look robust. If the system only looks good when the case already comes with abundant observability and dense candidates, then the bridge is not properly closed. It must be able to produce few candidates, many holds or blocks, central instrumentation gaps, and dominant baseline hardening without filling the case with weak pathways or ornamental pseudo-outputs.

phase4.rule.560.text: Phase 4 closes by sufficiency, not by exhaustiveness. This means that the MVP does not need to exhaust the entire verification vision of the framework in order to become methodologically complete. It only needs enough for the Verification Bridge to already exist as a serious layer of epistemic hardening, with central unit, explicit pathways, baseline hardening, instrumentation gaps, formal outcomes, and governable output contract.

phase4.rule.561.text: The following are not required in order to close the phase:

phase4.rule.562.text: strong verification executed with field data;

phase4.rule.563.text: full integration with historian or site metering;

phase4.rule.568.text: nor a complete institutional layer of external deliverables.

phase4.rule.569.text: Sufficiency does not impoverish the framework. It makes it buildable without pretending that the bridge is already the final verification layer.

phase4.rule.570.text: The following remain explicitly outside the Phase 4 MVP:

phase4.rule.573.text: operational historian integration as a constitutive closure requirement;

phase4.rule.574.text: sustained real logging or executed submetering;

phase4.rule.578.text: terminal evidence packages for third parties;

phase4.rule.580.text: and a national or fully institutionalized verification layer.

phase4.rule.581.text: All of that may belong to later scaling. None of it is a condition for declaring the phase closed as a serious MVP.

phase4.rule.582.text: What comes after the MVP is not simply “more of the same.” The next serious step of the framework enters a terrain where bridge architecture is no longer sufficient by itself and real site evidence starts becoming indispensable. The minimum bridge of the MVP organizes how a claim could harden; later scaling requires starting to materialize that hardening on real observability, data, and operation. In terms of maturation, the claim moves here from plausible claim to claim with a governed pathway; the next serious jump is already a claim contrasted against sufficient field data.

phase4.rule.583.text: Operational scaling introduces real observability conditions that the MVP does not need to have resolved in order to close, but that are necessary in order to rise to stronger verification. This includes, depending on the case:

phase4.rule.591.text: and, where needed, submetering or additional instrumentation.

phase4.rule.592.text: It also introduces very concrete site frictions: incomplete or badly named tags, historian with insufficient depth, partial export because of third-party restrictions, narrow maintenance windows, uptime constraints, shared boundaries between loads, and loss of operational context around overrides or manual modes. This scaling resolves one concrete problem: moving from plausible, well-designed pathways to pathways supported by sufficient real observation.

phase4.rule.593.text: Methodological scaling hardens the way the framework treats baseline, comparison, adjustment, uncertainty, and quantification. Here appear needs that the MVP does not have to exhaust:

phase4.rule.596.text: more serious adjustments over dominant variables;

phase4.rule.599.text: and more explicit, more worked uncertainty.

phase4.rule.600.text: This scaling resolves another problem: not just observing more, but observing in a way that supports harder and more quantitatively defensible inference.

phase4.rule.601.text: Institutional and verificatory scaling turns the architecture of the bridge into packages that are more auditable, more externalizable, and eventually more demanding in front of third parties. That terrain may include:

phase4.rule.603.text: verificatory deliverables usable by third parties;

phase4.rule.606.text: and, later on, a more continuous, more reproducible, or more standardized verification layer.

phase4.rule.607.text: That block does not belong to the MVP because it requires something the MVP still does not promise: field evidence strong enough, harder methodology, and, in many cases, greater institutionalization of output use.

phase4.rule.608.text: The next level of the framework does not exist by architectural will alone. It exists only when sufficient real evidence appears to put the pathway to the test against actual site operation. Depending on claim and case, this requires:

phase4.rule.612.text: historian, logging, or operational export where the pathway requires it;

phase4.rule.618.text: and, on many fronts, targeted measurement, short campaign, or delimited submetering.

phase4.rule.619.text: In other words: after the Verification Bridge MVP, the next serious step can no longer be achieved with more architecture alone. It is achieved when the designed architecture can meet field evidence strong enough to harden the claim, its baseline, and its domain of validity even further. In steam and district energy this usually requires more tightly closed thermal and measurement boundaries; in compressed air, load profiles and leak persistence; in power quality, sufficient resolution and event data; in BMS and controls, effective sequences, overrides, and trustworthy trends. That scaling does not replace candidate, pathway, evidence, baseline, instrumentation, and decision; it subjects them to a harder regime of observation, contrast, and real traceability.

phase4.rule.620.text: The closure of Phase 4 and the handoff to implementation do not require that the next stage already be built. They require that the semantics of the bridge can no longer be freely reinterpreted. Implementation receives a phase closed in its central units, outcomes, outputs, structural relationships, and minimum proof.

phase4.rule.621.text: That allows two things at once. First, to build the MVP without reopening candidate, pathway, baseline, instrumentation, or decision. Second, to prepare a reasonable continuity point toward later scaling when access to real field data exists. The correct handoff does not freeze one single software solution; it freezes semantics and leaves room for an implementation able to grow without betraying the bridge.
